      Where a passphrase gets its strength

      Strength comes from how the words are picked, not from how clever they look. FortiPass draws each word uniformly at random from the 7,776-word EFF large list with crypto.getRandomValues(), so every word adds log₂ 7,776 ≈ 12.9 bits — even if an attacker knows the list and your settings. Six words give about 77.5 bits; a number and a symbol add a few more.

      The crack times assume an offline attacker making 100 billion guesses per second against a fast hash — roughly one current high-end graphics card against MD5 or NTLM. An attacker with a rack of them is ten or a hundred times faster, so leave a margin. A site that stores passwords properly (bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2) slows any attacker down by many orders of magnitude.

      Passphrase or random password?

      • Use a passphrase for what you type by hand: your password manager's master password, your computer login, disk encryption, the Wi-Fi password you read out to guests.
      • Use a random password for everything a manager fills in: 16 or more random characters pack more bits into fewer keystrokes, and you never type them anyway.
      • Never pick the words yourself. People choose lyrics, quotes and words that belong together, and cracking dictionaries are full of them. The randomness is the whole point.

      About the word list

      The English list is the Electronic Frontier Foundation's large Diceware list: 7,776 common, concrete words chosen to be easy to spell and remember (7,776 = 6⁵, so five dice rolls pick one word). FortiPass removes the hyphen from four entries such as “t-shirt”, so that a hyphen separator always splits words unambiguously, and replaces the one duplicate this creates. Czech speakers can switch to the Czech version with Czech words.

      Questions people ask

      How many words should a passphrase have?

      Five words (about 64.6 bits) is fine for most online accounts behind a properly run login. Use six or more (77.5 bits and up) for anything an attacker could test offline: a password manager's master password, disk encryption or an encrypted backup.

      The word list is public — doesn't that make it weaker?

      No. The entropy figure already assumes the attacker has the exact list and knows how many words you used. The security comes from the random choice: with six words there are 7,776⁶ ≈ 2.2 × 10²³ equally likely passphrases.

      Do separators, capitals or a number make it stronger?

      A little. Capitalising every word is a single rule (about 1 bit), a fixed separator adds nothing an attacker would not try, and a random digit adds about 3.3 bits. One more word (12.9 bits) helps far more than any of them — they mostly exist to satisfy sites with composition rules.

      Is this the same as Diceware?

      Same idea and the same EFF list, with a cryptographic random number generator instead of dice. If you would rather trust physical dice, the EFF publishes the numbered list so you can roll your own.

      Are the passphrases sent or saved anywhere?

      No. Everything is generated in your browser tab with the Web Crypto API, and the page's Content Security Policy blocks every network request — open your browser's network panel and watch it stay empty. Only your settings are remembered on your device; generated values never are.
